clinicalPearls: Defined by a cardinal combination of progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, pharyngeal weakness causing dysphagia and dysarthria, and distal limb weakness.
Distal weakness (finger and wrist extensors, tibialis anterior with foot drop) is the key feature separating it from oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, which is proximal or limb-girdle in pattern.
Facial weakness is common and adds to the difficulty with speech and eye closure.
Onset is usually in early-to-mid adulthood with slow progression.
Disease linked to NOTCH2NLC overlaps with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease, so look for tremor, cognitive change, peripheral neuropathy or leukoencephalopathy.
Creatine kinase is normal or only mildly elevated.
Muscle biopsy characteristically shows rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions that stain for p62 and ubiquitin.
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, though apparently sporadic cases occur.
reference.pathophysiology: Oculopharyngodistal myopathy is a rare, genetically heterogeneous disorder caused by non-coding CGG trinucleotide repeat expansions in the 5' untranslated regions of several genes: LRP12 (OPDM1), GIPC1 (OPDM2), NOTCH2NLC (OPDM3, which overlaps mechanistically with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease) and RILPL1 (OPDM4). Disease is thought to result from a toxic RNA gain-of-function together with repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation of the expanded repeats, generating aggregation-prone polyglycine-containing proteins that form intranuclear inclusions. The resulting myopathy shows rimmed vacuoles and p62- and ubiquitin-positive intranuclear inclusions on biopsy. Although it resembles oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (caused by a short GCN triplet expansion in PABPN1), it is distinguished clinically by prominent distal limb involvement and genetically by its distinct non-coding repeat mechanism.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial disease with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
Myasthenia gravis with fatigable ptosis and ophthalmoplegia
Inclusion body myositis (rimmed vacuoles with distal and quadriceps weakness)
Distal myopathies such as GNE myopathy and Welander distal myopathy
additionalInvestigations: Repeat-expansion genetic testing for CGG expansions in LRP12, GIPC1, NOTCH2NLC and RILPL1, often requiring long-read sequencing or repeat-primed PCR.
Muscle biopsy for rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions.
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to confirm a myopathic process and detect any associated neuropathy.
Brain MRI, looking for leukoencephalopathy and corticomedullary diffusion-weighted hyperintensity that suggest the neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease overlap.
Repetitive nerve stimulation and acetylcholine receptor antibodies to exclude myasthenia gravis.
redFlags: Aspiration pneumonia or significant dysphagia with weight loss.
Respiratory muscle involvement or symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation.
Central nervous system features suggesting neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease, such as encephalopathic episodes or cognitive decline.
Rapidly progressive weakness, which should prompt reconsideration of an alternative diagnosis such as inclusion body myositis.
reference.prognosis: Progression is slow, typically over decades, and life expectancy may be near normal, but dysphagia-related aspiration and respiratory complications are the main threats. NOTCH2NLC-related disease carries additional neurological morbidity from its overlap with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease.
pitfalls: Easily misdiagnosed as oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis or mitochondrial ophthalmoplegia.
Standard exome or panel sequencing misses the non-coding CGG repeat expansions, so dedicated repeat testing (often long-read) is required.
Rimmed vacuoles overlap with inclusion body myositis and can lead to misdiagnosis.
The NOTCH2NLC overlap with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease and its central nervous system implications are easily overlooked.
Assuming a proximal pattern of weakness misses the distal involvement that is the key discriminator.
